lessons.title: Structuring Data with Lists and Tables
lessons.content:
Not all content is simple paragraphs. Often, data must be structured as lists or grids (tables).

### Lists
HTML supports three main types of lists:
1. **Unordered Lists (`<ul>`)**: Used for items where order doesn't matter (e.g., a shopping list). Items are marked with bullets. Each item is an `<li>` (List Item).
2. **Ordered Lists (`<ol>`)**: Used for numbered steps (e.g., a recipe). Each item is an `<li>`.
3. **Description Lists (`<dl>`)**: Used for key-value pairs (like a dictionary). Consists of `<dt>` (Description Term) and `<dd>` (Description Details).

### Tables
Tables represent tabular data in a grid. 
- `<table>`: The container for the table.
- `<tr>`: Table Row.
- `<th>`: Table Header (bold, centered by default). Used for column or row labels.
- `<td>`: Table Data (a standard cell).

**Advanced Table Structure:**
For large tables and accessibility, it is best practice to group rows semantically:
- `<thead>`: Wraps the header rows.
- `<tbody>`: Wraps the primary data rows.
- `<tfoot>`: Wraps summary or footer rows.

**Spanning Cells:**
To make a cell span multiple columns or rows, use the `colspan` and `rowspan` attributes on `<th>` or `<td>` elements.

lessons.title: Building Interactive Forms
lessons.content:
Forms are the primary way users send data to a web server.

### The `<form>` Element
The `<form>` tag acts as a container for input controls. Crucial attributes:
- `action`: The URL where the data is sent upon submission.
- `method`: The HTTP method used to send data (`GET` appends data to the URL, `POST` sends data invisibly in the request body—used for sensitive data).

### The `<input>` Element
The `<input>` tag is the most versatile form element. Its `type` attribute changes its behavior:
- `type="text"`: Standard text box.
- `type="password"`: Masks characters.
- `type="radio"`: Select one option from a group (must share the same `name`).
- `type="checkbox"`: Toggle multiple options.
- `type="email"`: Validates for email format.
- `type="submit"`: A button that submits the form.

### Labels and Accessibility
Every input should have an associated `<label>`. This is crucial for accessibility. The `for` attribute of the label must match the `id` attribute of the input.

### Other Controls
- `<textarea>`: For multi-line text input.
- `<select>` and `<option>`: Create a dropdown menu.
- `<fieldset>` and `<legend>`: Group related form elements and provide a caption.

lessons.title: Semantic Architecture and Accessibility Basics
lessons.content:
Semantic HTML means using HTML tags that convey the meaning of the content, rather than just how it should look. This is crucial for search engines (SEO) and screen readers (Accessibility).

### Semantic Structure Tags
Instead of using `<div>` for everything, HTML5 introduced tags that define the architecture of a page:
- `<header>`: The introductory content or navigation links at the top of a section/page.
- `<nav>`: A block of navigation links.
- `<main>`: The dominant content of the page.
- `<article>`: A self-contained, independent piece of content (like a blog post).
- `<section>`: A thematic grouping of content, typically with a heading.
- `<aside>`: Content tangentially related to the content around it (like a sidebar).
- `<footer>`: The footer for its nearest section/page.

### Accessibility (a11y) Fundamentals
Web accessibility ensures people with disabilities can use your site.
- **Alt Text**: Always provide descriptive `alt` attributes on images.
- **Heading Hierarchy**: Never skip heading levels (e.g., jumping from `<h1>` to `<h3>`). Screen readers use headings to navigate.
- **Keyboard Nav**: Interactive elements (links, buttons, inputs) must be focusable and operable via keyboard.

### ARIA Basics
ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) attributes help when native HTML isn't enough.
- `role`: Defines what an element is (e.g., `role="alert"`).
- `aria-label`: Provides an accessible name for an element when there is no visible text.
- `aria-hidden="true"`: Hides decorative elements from screen readers.

lessons.title: Native Validation and Complex Inputs
lessons.content:
HTML5 offers powerful built-in form validation, reducing the need for complex JavaScript for basic checks.

### Validation Attributes
- `required`: Forces the user to fill out the field before submitting.
- `minlength` and `maxlength`: Restricts the string length.
- `min` and `max`: Restricts the numerical or date range.
- `pattern`: Uses a Regular Expression (Regex) to validate the input (e.g., ensuring a zip code is 5 digits).
- `step`: Specifies the legal number intervals.

### Advanced Input Types
- `type="range"`: A slider control.
- `type="color"`: A color picker.
- `type="date"`, `type="time"`: Native date/time pickers.
- `type="file"`: Allows file uploads. (Remember: The `<form>` must have `enctype="multipart/form-data"`).

### Bypassing Validation
The `novalidate` attribute on a `<form>` tag tells the browser to skip native validation (often used when relying on custom JavaScript validation).

**Best Practice:** Client-side HTML validation improves User Experience (UX) by catching errors instantly, but you **must always** validate data on the server-side as well, because client-side HTML validation can easily be bypassed by a malicious user.

lessons.title: Page Architecture and SEO
lessons.content:
Building a real webpage requires combining elements into a logical, maintainable architecture while catering to search engines.

### The Viewport Meta Tag
To ensure your page renders correctly on mobile devices, you must include the viewport meta tag inside `<head>`:
`<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">`
This tells the browser to match the screen's width and set initial zoom to 1.

### SEO Fundamentals
Search Engine Optimization relies heavily on your HTML structure:
- **Title Tag**: The most important SEO element. Should be concise and descriptive.
- **Meta Description**: `<meta name="description" content="...">`. Shown as the snippet in Google results. Does not directly boost ranking, but boosts Click-Through Rate (CTR).
- **Heading Hierarchy**: Search engines use `<h1>`, `<h2>`, etc., to understand the topic of your page.

### Open Graph Basics
Open Graph (OG) meta tags control how your page appears when shared on social media (Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn).
- `<meta property="og:title" content="My Article">`
- `<meta property="og:image" content="image.jpg">`

### Reusable Patterns
A standard landing page usually consists of:
1. `<header>` (Logo, Nav)
2. `<main>` containing multiple `<section>`s (Hero, Features, Testimonials)
3. `<footer>` (Links, Copyright)

    <!-- Open Graph for Social Media -->
    <meta property="og:title" content="Super Widget 3000">
    <meta property="og:image" content="https://site.com/widget.jpg">

A professional HTML developer considers all of the following simultaneously when writing code:
1. **Validity**: Does it pass the W3C validator? Are all tags closed? Are attributes quoted correctly?
2. **Semantics**: Did I use the correct tag for the job? (`<nav>` for navigation, `<button>` for actions, `<a>` for links, `<main>` for core content).
3. **Accessibility (a11y)**: Can a screen reader understand this? Are there `alt` attributes? Is the heading hierarchy logical? Are form inputs tied to labels?
4. **Performance**: Are scripts deferred? Are images lazy-loaded? Are critical assets preloaded?
5. **SEO**: Is the `<title>` present? Are viewport and description `<meta>` tags configured? Are Open Graph tags set?

### Debugging HTML
When things look wrong, use the Browser Developer Tools (F12 or Right Click -> Inspect). You can view the rendered DOM, check computed styles, and see if tags were implicitly closed by the browser due to invalid nesting.
